metaDescription: Six electric lawn edgers, three corded 12 amp blade models and three cordless ones, compared on motor, blade size, depth and what a cord really costs you.
expertTake: The WORX WG896 is the pick for most small to mid sized yards because its 12 amp motor and 4700 rpm blade give real cutting power with no battery to maintain. The Black+Decker 12 Amp trencher is the value pick, and doubles as a shallow trench digger. Skip the corded models if your edges are far from an outlet, since an extension cord across a driveway is a hazard and a nuisance.
introParagraphs: Electric edgers come in two flavors. Corded models run on household power and deliver steady output for as long as you have cord, while cordless models trade that endless runtime for freedom from the cable.

The choice shapes everything else: weight, noise, how deep a trench the tool can dig, and what you will fuss with in year three. This guide sets both styles side by side so you can match the power source to the layout of your yard.

products.name: WORX WG896 12 Amp 7.5 Inch Corded Lawn Edger and Trencher
products.description:
Twelve amps drives a 7.5 inch blade at 4700 rpm, a spec that tells you the motor is built for work, not just for show. Three depth settings of 1, 1.25 and 1.5 inches match the cut to the turf, and a cutting line indicator helps you hold a straight track along a walk.

Being corded, it needs no battery and starts on every pull, so it is the least fussy tool here once you accept a cord. A small to mid sized yard with an outlet near the work is where it makes sense. Compared with the Black+Decker it has the cutting line indicator and a clearly stated speed, and compared with the cordless models it is cheaper to own over time.

Handle the cord like a tool, not an afterthought: keep it behind you, clear of the blade, and use a rated outdoor extension. Brush soil from the housing after use and inspect the blade for rounding. Because corded edgers deliver full power the moment you squeeze the trigger, rest the blade on the grass line before you start, let it reach speed and then lower the wheel, which gives a cleaner entry cut than plunging into a dense mat of turf. Wear closed shoes and eye protection, since the blade throws grit sideways.
products.bestFor: Small to mid sized yards with an outlet near the edges.
pros: Cutting line indicator for straight tracks
No battery to buy or charge
cons: Cord limits reach and needs managing
Extension cord across paths is a trip hazard

products.name: BLACK+DECKER 12 Amp 7.5 Inch Lawn Edger and Trencher 2 in 1

specList.label: Extra use
specList.value: Shallow trenching for cable and irrigation

products.description:
This edger is built with a second job in mind: the listing says it can dig shallow trenches for cable, wire and irrigation lines, as well as edge along driveways and patios. The same 12 amp motor and 7.5 inch blade handle both tasks, so the tool earns its keep beyond edging season.

The tradeoff is that a trencher is a blunt tool. A blade that digs a narrow trench through grass is not as refined as a dedicated edger, and the control is less about a razor edge and more about a clean slot. Against the WORX WG896 it matches the motor and blade size at a lower price tier, but gives up the cutting line indicator.

Support the cord, work in dry soil and clear stones from the path, because a pebble kicked at a spinning blade will chip it. Rinse mud from the housing after use and let it dry. When you trench, make the first pass at the shallowest depth and widen the slot on a second pass, because a deep single cut through clay can bind the blade and trip the motor. Call your utility locator before digging near buried lines.
products.bestFor: Gardeners who also want to trench for cable or irrigation lines.
pros: Edges and trenches with one tool
cons: Trenching blade is less refined for edging

products.name: CRAFTSMAN CMEED400 12 Amp Corded Lawn Edger
products.description:
The adjustable auxiliary handle is what distinguishes this edger: you set the second grip for your height and reach, which reduces the stoop that gives many people a sore back after twenty minutes. A 12 amp high torque motor handles tough turf, and the line cutting guide helps you hold a straight path along hard surfaces.

It is described as suited to both edging and trenching, so it shares the dual role of the Black+Decker. Compared with the WORX it adds the adjustable handle, and compared with a cordless model it never runs flat.

Keep the cord clipped to a belt loop or looped over a shoulder, and replace a nicked cord immediately. Brush soil from the guard, inspect the blade and check the handle clamp for tightness each season. The auxiliary handle is also the right place to hang the cord loop, which keeps the cable off the ground in front of you and makes the pass along a long drive far less awkward.
products.bestFor: Taller or shorter users who need an adjustable second grip.

products.name: Greenworks 40V 8 Inch Brushless Edger Kit, 4.0Ah battery

specList.label: Guide
specList.value: Curb wheel and tool free depth

products.description:
For anyone who dislikes cords, this brushless 40V kit is the electric answer. A 4.0Ah battery and charger are in the box, the 8 inch steel blade rides a curb wheel, and tool free depth adjustment lets you change the cut without a wrench. The brushless motor runs cool and is quieter than a brushed one.

Runtime is bounded by the battery, which is the key tradeoff against the corded models. A short driveway edge fits easily on one charge, and a very long border may need a second pack. Against the WORX WG896 it frees you from the cord and offers a larger blade, but it costs far more.

Remove the battery after each use and store it indoors partly charged. Scrape soil from the blade housing, since a caked housing is the main cause of overheating. On a long border, set the first pass at a middle depth and finish with a lighter pass, so the brushless motor never spends a whole pack grinding through roots.
products.bestFor: Yards with edges far from an outlet and a desire to avoid cords.
cons: 40V platform does not share with other brands

products.name: goodjob 20V Cordless Lawn Edger, 9 inch blade, 2 batteries
products.description:
Two batteries and a fast charger in the box mean you can swap and keep going, which counters the main cordless worry. A 400W motor spins a 9 inch blade at 3500 rpm, and dual guide wheels with three depths give stability and control.

The 9 inch blade gives more reach than the corded tools, but the 400W motor has less raw power than a 12 amp corded machine. It is a newer brand, so long term service is less certain. Against the Greenworks kit it costs far less and has a bigger blade, but lacks a brushless motor and a name brand.

Charge both packs after use, keep the blade clean and check the blade fastener for tightness every few uses. Store the tool dry. Because the motor is rated at a modest wattage, favor shallow, repeated passes over one deep bite, which keeps the pack from sagging and gives a more even edge.
products.bestFor: Cordless users who want two batteries on a budget.
pros: Two batteries and a fast charger
cons: Lower power than 12 amp corded tools

products.name: VEVOR 8.8 Inch Cordless Lawn Edger, 20V, 4000mAh battery
products.description:
The VEVOR has three clearly stated depth settings of 1, 1.25 and 1.5 inches, an 8.8 inch blade, and a 4000mAh pack that spins it up to 3200 rpm. It is a straightforward, lower cost cordless edger, aimed at small yards with short edges.

The pack is one battery, so a long job may need a recharge before you finish. The depth tops out at 1.5 inches, which is the same as the corded WORX, but with less motor power behind it. One pack instead of the goodjob's two, and a lower price for it.

Remove the battery after use, brush soil off the housing and keep the blade in good condition. Store the tool dry and charged to about half. If your lawn has a lot of stones along the driveway, sweep the line first, because a stone thrown by a thin blade can chip it and leave a rough cut for the rest of the season.
products.bestFor: Small yards with short edges and a lower budget.

buyingCriteria.explanation: A 12 amp corded motor like the WORX WG896 spins at 4700 rpm for as long as you have power and never fades. A 20V cordless unit such as the VEVOR trades that for freedom of movement. For a yard with an outlet near the work, corded wins on cost and power. For long, remote edges, cordless wins on convenience.

A corded motor is rated in amps, a cordless one in volts and watts, and the numbers do not compare directly. The WORX and Craftsman list 12 amps, while the goodjob lists 400W. At household voltage, 12 amps is well above 1000 watts, so the corded tools have far more sustained power than a 400W cordless one. That gap shows up in thick, compacted soil and along a curb with a heavy thatch, where a smaller motor slows and the cut gets ragged.

A larger blade reaches deeper, but depth is capped by the adjustment. The 7.5 inch corded tools reach 1.5 inches, the 8 inch Greenworks cuts deeper and the goodjob has a 9 inch blade. For restoring an old edge you need depth, and for maintenance you need only a clean slice.

A cord needs a plan: keep it behind you, use an outdoor rated extension and never run it across the blade side. The corded tools here are only as good as your outlet layout. If the yard is large, cord handling becomes the main time sink. A practical rule is to plan your route so that you always walk away from the outlet along the edge and return along the other side, which keeps the cord in grass you have already finished and never across a fresh cut.

The Black+Decker and Craftsman list shallow trenching as a use. A trenching blade is thicker and blunter, so it digs a slot rather than slicing a crisp wall. If you only edge, a thinner dedicated blade is better. If you also bury cable, a trencher saves a tool.

The Craftsman has an adjustable auxiliary handle, and the Greenworks has a curb wheel for tracking. A tool that fits your height reduces back strain. Try the handle at a store if you can, since an uncomfortable edger gets used less. Look at where the switch sits and whether a left handed grip is awkward, because you hold the tool in one position for a long time.

howWeEvaluated.title: Motor power
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared 12 amp corded motors with cordless watt ratings. The three corded tools led on sustained power, while the Greenworks brushless motor led among cordless ones.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cut capability
howWeEvaluated.description: Blade size and depth range were compared. The Greenworks 8 inch and goodjob 9 inch blades led among cordless units, and the 7.5 inch corded blades matched on depth.

howWeEvaluated.title: Convenience
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed cord management against battery management. The corded tools need no charging, and the cordless kits need a pack.

howWeEvaluated.title: Control and handling
howWeEvaluated.description: Handle design, guide lines and wheels were reviewed. The Craftsman adjustable handle and the Greenworks curb wheel scored well.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value
howWeEvaluated.description: The priceTier ran from low cost corded models to a mid price cordless kit. Based on the spec sheet and owner feedback patterns, corded tools gave the most power per unit cost, and the cordless tools gave the most convenience per minute of use. We also noted that the corded tools have fewer parts to age, which counts for a lot in year three.

cards.label: Corded
cards.text: More sustained power for less money and no battery to maintain, but a cord to manage. Picks: WORX WG896, BLACK+DECKER 12 Amp and CRAFTSMAN CMEED400.

cards.label: Cordless
cards.text: Freedom to roam and no trip hazard, but less sustained power and a battery to charge. Picks: Greenworks 40V Kit, goodjob 20V and VEVOR 8.8 Inch.

howToChoose.note: Choose corded if you have outlets nearby and want power for less, and cordless for far edges.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A light tool, a shallow depth range and easy storage. Short edges do not need a big battery or a long cord.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The WORX WG896 and the VEVOR 8.8 Inch are the small yard choices, depending on whether you prefer a cord.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You hate cords or have long edges. The Greenworks 40V Kit is the cordless answer.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: Your edges are near an outlet. The corded tools give more power per unit cost.

maintenance.why: A nicked cord is a shock hazard. Replace damaged cords and use an outdoor rated extension.
Packed soil overheats the motor and slows the blade.
Concrete rounds the cutting edge. A dull blade tears grass and strains the motor.
Loose wheels and clamps cause wobble and uneven cuts.
Storage at roughly half charge, somewhere cool, is what these cells want.

faq.q: Is a corded electric edger better than cordless?
faq.a: Corded tools offer more sustained power for less money, while cordless ones offer freedom. Choose by your outlet layout.

faq.q: How do I manage the cord?
faq.a: Keep it behind you and clear of the blade, use a rated outdoor extension and clip it to your belt if you can.

faq.q: Can an edger dig a trench?
faq.a: Some can, to a shallow depth. The Black+Decker and Craftsman list trenching, but a trencher is blunter than a dedicated edger.

faq.q: How deep can electric edgers cut?
faq.a: The corded 7.5 inch tools cut up to 1.5 inches. Larger 8 inch tools can cut deeper.

faq.q: How long does an edger blade last?
faq.a: It depends on the surface. Concrete wears blades quickly, so replace them when the edge rounds.

faq.q: Is an electric edger safe to use in damp grass?
faq.a: Avoid wet ground with a corded tool and use a GFCI protected outlet. Cordless tools are safer in damp conditions but still need care.
